approachQuestion.prompt:
Packing captions. Given a read-only array parts of n strings, return one string containing their characters in the original array order with no separators. Empty strings are allowed. Let L be the total number of characters. There are 1 <= n <= 100,000 strings and 0 <= L <= 200,000 characters; each character is a fixed-size code unit. String lengths are stored and readable directly. Return an owning flat string, not a rope, view, or list of chunks. Choose minimum worst-case total time, breaking equal-time ties by smaller auxiliary storage.

Example 1: Input: parts=["ab","","C","de"]. Output: "abCde".
Example 2: Input: parts=["",""]. Output: "".

The output API can allocate a flat result with a chosen length, initialize it, fill its character positions, and seal that same allocation as the returned string without copying. Allocating/initializing k characters and copying k characters each take work proportional to k. Concatenating two immutable strings creates a new flat string and copies both operands. Inputs cannot be modified.

options.text: Sum the stored string lengths, allocate the result at that exact length, then copy each part directly into its successive positions and seal it.
options.feedback: The total length determines the single output allocation. Each character is copied into its final position, and empty parts preserve order without contributing characters.

options.text: Sum the lengths, allocate a separate character array of that length, fill it with all parts, then allocate and copy it into the returned flat string.
options.feedback: This works for every input and has optimal total growth in running time, but the temporary full array is avoidable with the supplied output API.

options.text: Start with an empty immutable string and repeatedly replace it with the concatenation of the accumulated string and the next part.
options.feedback: The content is correct, but each concatenation recopies the accumulated prefix. For n one-character parts, it copies prefixes of lengths 1,2,...,n instead of writing each character directly to its final slot.

options.text: Sort the parts lexicographically, then concatenate them in that order.
options.feedback: Sorting changes the required order. For parts=["z","a"], it returns "az" rather than "za".

feedback.reason: Include the cost of copying growing values and distinguish required output storage from temporary copies.
details: Read all stored lengths to obtain L. Allocate the flat output for L characters. Traverse parts in order and copy each character to the next output slot, keeping a write offset. Seal this same allocation as the result. No separate character collection or accumulated immutable prefix is created.

Empty parts contribute no characters but still have stored lengths to inspect. Writing directly into the final allocation avoids repeatedly copying an ever-longer immutable prefix. This constant-helper-space result depends on sealing the same allocation; converting a separate buffer by copying would count that buffer as auxiliary.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For size-once-fill-output, what are worst-case time and peak auxiliary space in terms of the number n of parts and total character count L? Count length reads, output allocation/initialization, and character copies. The allocation returned after sealing is required output throughout construction and is excluded from auxiliary space.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

options.text: O(n + L) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n + L) time, O(L + 1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Inspect n part headers and write L characters directly into returned storage.
details: Reading lengths and visiting parts cost O(n), even for empty strings. Initialization and copying cost O(L), giving O(n + L). Only lengths, offsets, and loop counters remain outside the required result; the input is never copied and no recursion is used. Repeated immutable concatenation has extra prefix-copy work, but the analyzed method writes directly into the final allocation.
“O(L + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Empty parts still require length reads and traversal. With L=0, n can still be large.
“O(n + L) time, O(L + 1) auxiliary space”: The L-character allocation is the required result, explicitly excluded. No second character buffer exists.
“O(n(L + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This loose upper bound includes repeated accumulated-prefix copying, which this method avoids; n+L is tighter.
